source: The 400 Investment Banking Interview Questions & Answers You Need to Know

items.prompt_mdx: What are the most common multiples used in valuation?

solution.model_answer_mdx: **EV/Revenue**, **EV/EBITDA**, **EV/EBIT**, **P/E** (share price over earnings per share) and P/BV (share price over book value per share).

items.prompt_mdx: What are some examples of industry-specific multiples?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Internet: EV per unique **visitors** or pageviews. Retail and airlines: EV/**EBITDAR**, which removes rent because it is large and varies with the lease-versus-own choice. Energy: price over reserves or daily production, and P/NAV. REITs: Price/**FFO** and Price/AFFO, where FFO adds back depreciation and removes gains on property sales to show normalised cash flow.

items.prompt_mdx: With an industry multiple like EV / Scientists or EV / Subscribers, why use Enterprise Value rather than Equity Value?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Because those scientists or subscribers generate value for **all investors**, lenders and shareholders alike. The test for any multiple is to ask which investors the denominator is available to.

items.prompt_mdx: Why can't you use Equity Value / EBITDA as a multiple instead of Enterprise Value / EBITDA?

solution.model_answer_mdx: EBITDA is earned before interest, so it belongs to **all investors**. Enterprise Value covers the same perimeter. Equity Value only reflects the **equity** holders' share of the capital structure, so pairing it with EBITDA mixes two perimeters.

items.prompt_mdx: With Free Cash Flow multiples, do you use Equity Value or Enterprise Value?

solution.model_answer_mdx: It depends on the cash flow. **Unlevered** Free Cash Flow is before interest and goes to all investors, so it pairs with Enterprise Value. **Levered** Free Cash Flow is after interest, lenders have been paid, so it pairs with Equity Value.

items.prompt_mdx: You never use Equity Value / EBITDA. Are there cases where you might use Equity Value / Revenue?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Very rarely. Large **financial institutions** with big cash balances can show **negative** Enterprise Values, so a revenue multiple on Equity Value may be shown instead, for example on a slide mixing financial and non-financial companies. For banks you would normally rely on P/E and P/BV anyway.

items.prompt_mdx: How do you select Comparable Companies and Precedent Transactions?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Three screens: **industry**, **financial** criteria such as revenue or EBITDA size, and **geography**. Industry is always used. For transactions you also limit by date, typically the last one to two years.

items.prompt_mdx: How do you apply the 3 valuation methodologies to actually get a value for the company? Illustrate with a median precedent multiple of 8x EBITDA and EBITDA of 500 million USD.

solution.model_answer_mdx: Take the **median** multiple of the peer set or transaction set and multiply it by the company's own metric. Here 8 x 500 million = **4 billion** USD of implied Enterprise Value. For a football field, also use the minimum, maximum, 25th and 75th percentiles to build a range.

items.prompt_mdx: Why would a company with similar growth and profitability to its Comparable Companies be valued at a premium?

solution.model_answer_mdx: It may have just beaten **earnings** expectations, hold a **competitive advantage** not visible in the numbers such as a key patent, have won a major lawsuit, or be the **market leader** with a larger share than peers.

items.prompt_mdx: What are the flaws with public company comparables?

solution.model_answer_mdx: No two companies are truly **comparable**. The stock **market** is emotional, so multiples swing with sentiment. And small, **thinly** traded stocks may not reflect full value.

items.prompt_mdx: How do you take a company's competitive advantage into account in a valuation?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Use the **75th percentile** of multiples instead of the median, add a **premium** to some multiples, or use more aggressive **projections**. In practice you pick one, not all three.

items.prompt_mdx: Do you always use the median multiple of a set of comparables or precedent transactions?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Usually, since you want the middle of the range. But for a **distressed** or underperforming company you might use the **25th percentile**, and a higher percentile for an outperformer.

items.prompt_mdx: Precedent Transactions usually give a higher value than Comparable Companies. When might that not be the case?

solution.model_answer_mdx: When there is a **mismatch** between the M&A market and the public market, for instance no recent takeovers of listed companies but many small **private** companies bought at very low valuations.

items.prompt_mdx: What are some flaws with precedent transactions?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Past deals are rarely fully **comparable**: structure, size and market sentiment differ. And **data** is harder to find than for listed peers, especially for small private targets.

items.prompt_mdx: Two companies with the same financial profile are bought by the same acquirer, but one EBITDA multiple is twice the other. How could this happen?

solution.model_answer_mdx: One sale process was more **competitive**, with more bidders. One target had recent **bad news** or a depressed share price and went at a discount. Or they sit in **industries** with different median multiples.

items.prompt_mdx: Why does Warren Buffett prefer EBIT multiples to EBITDA multiples?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Because EBITDA ignores **capital expenditures**, which are a real and often large cost of staying in business. In capital-intensive industries the gap between EBIT and EBITDA is wide and EBITDA flatters the picture.

items.prompt_mdx: EV/EBIT, EV/EBITDA and P/E all measure profitability. What is the difference and when do you use each?

solution.model_answer_mdx: P/E depends on **capital structure**, the two EV multiples do not. So P/E suits **banks** and other companies where interest is central. EV/EBIT is after **D&A**, EV/EBITDA before: use EV/EBIT where fixed assets and capex matter, as in manufacturing, and EV/EBITDA where they matter less, as in internet businesses.

items.prompt_mdx: You are buying a vending machine business. Would you pay a higher multiple if it owns its machines and depreciates them, or if it leases them? Depreciation and lease cost are the same amount and everything else is equal.

solution.model_answer_mdx: A **higher** EV/EBITDA multiple for the one that **leases**. Enterprise Value is the same in both cases, but the lease cost sits above **EBITDA** while depreciation sits below it. The leasing company therefore reports lower EBITDA, which mechanically gives a higher multiple.

items.prompt_mdx: It is April and you are looking at a comparable company's financials. How do you calendarize them to show the Trailing Twelve Months rather than the last fiscal year?

solution.model_answer_mdx: TTM = **most recent fiscal year** + new **partial period** - same partial period of the prior year. Here: last fiscal year plus Q1 of this year minus Q1 of last year. Quarterly figures come from quarterly filings or interim reports.

items.prompt_mdx: Walk me through an M&A premiums analysis. Illustrate with a company trading at 10.00 USD per share acquired at 15.00 USD.

solution.model_answer_mdx: It measures the **premium** buyers paid over sellers' share prices in similar deals. Here 15 / 10 - 1 = **50%**. Steps: select transactions by industry, date and size. For each, take the seller's share price 1, 20 and 60 days before announcement and compute the premium against each. Take the **median** of each series and apply it to your company's corresponding share prices. It only works for public targets.

items.prompt_mdx: M&A premiums analysis and precedent transactions both look at past deals. How does the selection differ?

solution.model_answer_mdx: For premiums, every seller must be **public**. The set is also **broader**: perhaps fewer than ten precedent transactions but dozens of premiums, with looser industry and financial screens. Otherwise the criteria are similar: financials, industry, geography, date.

items.prompt_mdx: You need projections from equity research for a set of comparables. How do you choose which report to use?

solution.model_answer_mdx: Two common rules: the most **detailed** report, or the one whose numbers sit in the **middle** of the range. You do not choose by the bank that wrote it. Using only your own bank's research would undermine objectivity.

items.prompt_mdx: You have a set of precedent transactions but are missing data like EBITDA for many targets. Where do you look?

solution.model_answer_mdx: **Press** releases and financial press articles. Then **equity research** on the buyer around the deal date, where analysts may estimate the seller's figures. Then data providers such as **Capital IQ** or FactSet.

items.prompt_mdx: How far back and forward do you usually go for comparable and precedent multiples?

solution.model_answer_mdx: **TTM** for both, plus one or two years **forward**. For listed peers you may look further in both directions. For transactions, going more than one year forward is unusual because information is limited.

items.prompt_mdx: One company has a 40% EBITDA margin and trades at 8x EBITDA. Another has a 10% margin and trades at 16x. What is the problem with comparing them directly?

solution.model_answer_mdx: It is not forbidden, but **misleading**: by simple arithmetic the high-**margin** company will tend to show a lower EBITDA multiple regardless of its real worth. Better to screen on margins and drop the **outliers**. You would not try to normalise multiples for margins.
